landmarks.name: Leptis Magna
landmarks.writeup: An ancient Roman city on the coast, known for its well-preserved ruins including a theater, basilica, and marketplace.

wiki.extract: Leptis or Lepcis Magna, also known by other names in antiquity, was a prominent city of the Carthaginian Empire and Roman Libya at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda in the Mediterranean.

landmarks.name: Cyrene
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site featuring Greek and Roman ruins, including temples and a necropolis.

wiki.extract: Cyrene, also sometimes anglicized as Kyrene, was an ancient Greek colony and Roman city near present-day Shahhat in northeastern Libya in North Africa. It was part of the Pentapolis, an important group of five cities in the region, and gave the area its classical and early modern name Cyrenaica.

landmarks.name: Sabratha
landmarks.writeup: An ancient Roman city with impressive ruins such as a theater and forum, located on the Mediterranean coast.

wiki.extract: Sabratha, in the Zawiya District of Libya, was the westernmost of the ancient "three cities" of Roman Tripolis, alongside Oea and Leptis Magna. From 2001 to 2007 it was the capital of the former Sabratha wa Sorman District. It lies on the Mediterranean coast about 70 km (43 mi) west of modern Tripoli. The extant archaeological site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

landmarks.name: Ghadames
landmarks.writeup: A historic Berber town known as the 'Pearl of the Desert' with traditional mud-brick architecture.

wiki.extract: Ghadames or Ghadamis is an oasis town in the Nalut District of the Tripolitania region in northwestern Libya.

landmarks.name: Acacus Mountains
landmarks.writeup: A mountain range famous for prehistoric rock art dating back thousands of years.

wiki.extract: The Acacus Mountains or Tadrart Akakus form a mountain range in the desert of the Ghat District in western Libya, part of the Sahara. They are situated east of the city of Ghat, Libya, and stretch north from the border with Algeria, about 100 kilometres (62 mi). The area has a particularly rich array of prehistoric rock art.

cultural_events.name: Libyan Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on December 24th, marking Libya's independence from Italy in 1951.

wiki.extract: An Independence Day is an annual event commemorating the anniversary of a nation's independence or statehood, usually after ceasing to be a group or part of another nation or state, or after the end of a military occupation, or after a major change in government. Many countries commemorate their independence from a colonial empire.

cultural_events.name: Eid al-Fitr
cultural_events.writeup: A major Islamic festival marking the end of Ramadan, celebrated with feasts and communal prayers.

wiki.extract: Eid al-Fitr is the first of the two main festivals in Islam, the other being Eid al-Adha. The holiday falls on the first day of Shawwal, the tenth month of the Islamic calendar. One of the most important Islamic celebrations, Eid al-Fitr is celebrated by Muslims worldwide as it marks the end of the month-long, dawn-to-dusk fasting (sawm) during Ramadan. The holiday is known under various other names in different languages and countries around the world.

cultural_events.name: Eid al-Adha
cultural_events.writeup: An important Islamic holiday commemorating the willingness of Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, observed with prayers and animal sacrifice.

wiki.extract: Eid al-Adha is the second of the two main festivals in Islam, alongside Eid al-Fitr. It falls on the 10th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the twelfth and final month of the Islamic calendar. Celebrations and observances are generally carried forward to the three following days, known as the Tashreeq days.

food_writeup: Libyan cuisine features Mediterranean and North African influences, with staple dishes like couscous, bazin (a type of bread), and shakshouka. Meals often include lamb, dates, olives, and spices such as cumin and coriander.
brief_history: Libya has a rich history influenced by indigenous Berber cultures, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, and Arab civilizations. It was an Italian colony from 1911 until World War II. Libya gained independence in 1951, later ruled by Muammar Gaddafi from 1969 until 2011. Since then, the country has experienced political instability and conflict.

commentary.inflation_management: Libya's inflation reflects war, currency crisis, and oil blockades rather than monetary policy. It was low before 2011 (1.5-2.5% in 2006, 2009-10), then spiked to 15.9% in 2011 as the revolution disrupted supply. The 2014-16 oil blockade and dinar collapse drove inflation to 25.9% in 2016 and 25.8% in 2017, the series highs, as the parallel exchange rate soared. A 2020 devaluation and ceasefire stabilized prices: -2.2% in 2019, then 1-5% from 2020, with a projected 1.8% in 2025. The central bank remains split between rival authorities, so monetary policy is effectively absent; inflation is determined by oil flows and the parallel market.
commentary.debt_management: Libya has no published public debt series in the IMF data: the gross debt field is blank for the entire 2006-2025 period, reflecting the fragmentation of the state and the absence of consolidated fiscal accounts since 2011. What is known is that Libya entered the crisis with virtually no debt and massive reserves, and that rival governments in Tripoli and the east have since spent heavily on conflict, subsidies, and parallel budgets, financed by oil revenues and central bank advances. The lack of data is itself the story: without unified accounts, debt sustainability cannot be assessed, and the risk is of hidden liabilities accumulating in the institutional vacuum.

key_events.event: Revolution ousted and killed Muammar Qaddafi (October 2011); GDP in USD terms peaked at $92.5bn in 2012 on the oil rebound.
Civil war split the country; oil blockades crashed production and revenues.
Battle for Tripoli (2019-20) further devastated the economy; inflation hit 25%+ on currency collapse.
Ceasefire and unity government; oil production recovered; dinar devalued to unify rates.
Storm Daniel caused catastrophic flooding in Derna (September 2023), killing thousands.
Political stalemate persisted with rival governments; elections repeatedly postponed.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The outlook is political, not economic: Libya's oil wealth could fund rapid recovery, but only a unified government can produce a budget, a debt account, or a monetary policy. The base case is continued stalemate with oil keeping the economy afloat and inflation low. Upside is reunification unlocking investment; downside is renewed war or oil shutdowns. Uncertainty is very high, and the absence of fiscal data means even the starting position is unknown.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections. Note: the IMF publishes no general government gross debt series for Libya.
